ocar.opportunity: Serial-section electron microscopy can reconstruct neural circuits, and convolutional nets have reached impressive accuracy on clean images. Computational systems are being built to handle petavoxel images of cubic-millimeter brain volumes.
ocar.challenge: Image analysis was manual for half a century; even recent ssEM reconstructions took tens of thousands of hours. ssEM images carry damaged sections, misalignments, and poor axial resolution compared with FIB-SEM.
ocar.action: Lee, Turner, Macrina, Wu, Lu and Seung, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), review convolutional nets for neuronal boundary detection and for synapses, partner identity, extending or pruning reconstructions, and serial-section alignment.
ocar.resolution: Accuracy on clean images is high, but remaining errors still need human proofreading. The authors argue that as volumes grow, total human effort may increase even as per-voxel automation improves; a cubic millimeter had not yet been fully reconstructed.
ocar.future_work: Robust handling of image defects is the outstanding challenge. They expect cubic-millimeter ssEM to become routine, while cubic-centimeter (whole mouse brain) volumes may require new block-face methods; the contest between ssEM and block-face EM continues.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue are still often pieced into circuits by people, a slow job. This review explains how convolutional neural networks now trace cells, find synapses, and line up serial images—and why messy images remain hard.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2019), Lee, Turner, Macrina, Wu, Lu and Seung survey convolutional nets for reconstructing circuits from serial-section EM. Nets first used for boundary detection a dozen years earlier now do well on clean images, and are also used to find synapses and partners, extend or prune traces, and align sections into 3D stacks. They contrast defect-prone ssEM with isotropic 8 nm FIB-SEM chosen at Janelia for a fly connectome. Systems are being engineered for petavoxel, cubic-millimeter volumes.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a new benchmark. ‘Impressive accuracy on clean images’ is qualitative; robust defect handling is explicitly unsolved. Claims about FIB-SEM being the cheapest fly-connectome route rest on personal communication. The cubic-millimeter scale statement is historical as of 2019.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue are still often pieced into circuits by people, a slow job. This review explains how convolutional neural networks now trace cells, find synapses, and line up serial images—and why messy images remain hard.

ocar.opportunity: As EM connectomics datasets grow, the field needs the equivalent of git: publish a snapshot, let remote collaborators branch it, and merge accepted edits back with provenance.
ocar.challenge: Connectome generation is rate-limited by segmentation quality and proofreading. Volume EM reconstructions are hard to distribute as files, and snapshot publication does not support collaborative editing of the same huge labeled volume.
ocar.action: Katz and Plaza, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2019), present DVID, a web-based connectomics API with distributed versioning. It is the central data resource for Janelia’s FlyEM team, with backends from local SSDs to cloud object stores.
ocar.resolution: Branched, versioned data supports proofreader training and segmentation experiments. Storage is tailored by data type for efficient queries. The system deploys from laptops to large servers and is open source.
ocar.future_work: They plan git-like offline proofreading of regions of interest on laptops with pull requests, and merge tools so separate DVID servers can scale proofreading without enlarging a single machine.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope brain maps are hard to share and edit as a team. This paper describes DVID, software that versions those maps like git versions code, so people can branch, proofread, and merge changes.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2019), Katz and Plaza introduce DVID (Distributed Versioned Image-Oriented Dataservice). Analogous to GitHub, it offers a web connectomics API so collaborators can branch EM datasets and reintegrate edits. Used as FlyEM’s central store, it versions proofreading and segmentation experiments and persists to SSDs or cloud object stores. Backend choice is matched to each data type for storage efficiency and fast queries. It is freely available as open source.
summaries.advanced: The paper is a technology report of a deployed system, not a controlled benchmark against other dataservices. ‘First steps toward distributed versioning’ is the authors’ framing; full git-style merge of arbitrary remote edits is still aspirational. Reviewers included other connectomics software authors; independent scale numbers beyond the FlyEM deployment are not given here.

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope brain maps are hard to share and edit as a team. This paper describes DVID, software that versions those maps like git versions code, so people can branch, proofread, and merge changes.

ocar.opportunity: A whole-animal Drosophila connectome needs the brain, connectives, and ventral nerve cord as one specimen, imaged at synapse resolution with contrast high enough for automated membrane and synapse detection.
ocar.challenge: The intact CNS is too large for flash freezing. Conventional aldehyde fixation often flattens neurites, which hurts machine segmentation, and FIB-SEM has historically been slow.
ocar.action: Lu, Xu, Hayworth, Rivlin, Plaza, Scheffer, Rubin, Hess and Meinertzhagen, in a 2019 bioRxiv preprint, report a dissection jig, Durcupan embedment with hot-knife slicing, heavy-metal contrast, and progressive-lowering-of-temperature dehydration for en bloc fly CNS.
ocar.resolution: Neurites are recovered as round profiles with dark synapses, suited to machine segmentation and automated synapse detection with little human help. They image at a usual 8 nm per voxel and report a Drosophila brain FIB-SEM stack eight times faster than before, at about serial-section rates without cutting artifacts.
ocar.future_work: They suggest still-higher contrast, gas-cluster milling, and multi-beam SEM. Dissection severs sensory axons, leaving degenerating afferents. Component steps such as BSA coating for hot-knife slicing may transfer to other species.

summaries.beginner: To map an entire fruit-fly nervous system, the brain and cord must be dissected, stained, and imaged as one piece. This methods paper shows how to prepare that specimen so a FIB-SEM microscope can collect synapse-ready images much faster than before.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (2019), Lu, Xu, Hayworth, Meinertzhagen and Janelia colleagues tackle three preparation bottlenecks for a Drosophila FIB-SEM connectome: contiguous dissection of brain plus ventral nerve cord, fixation of a sample too large for flash freezing, and contrast for fast synapse detection. A custom jig, Durcupan embedment with hot-knife slicing, heavy metals, and progressive-lowering-of-temperature dehydration yield round neurites and dark synapses at a usual 8 nm per voxel. They report an eight-fold speedup of brain FIB-SEM, approaching serial-section rates without sectioning artifacts. Automated synapse counts are said to match human proofreaders.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods preprint, not a released whole-brain connectome. ‘Eight times faster’ is the authors’ comparison to prior FIB-SEM, not a head-to-head with all ssEM platforms. Matching human synapse counts cites Shinomiya et al. (2019), not a full census in this extract. Catalog tags mention VNC datasets; the text emphasizes connected sub- and supraesophageal ganglia after hot-knife slicing.

plain_language_summary: To map an entire fruit-fly nervous system, the brain and cord must be dissected, stained, and imaged as one piece. This methods paper shows how to prepare that specimen so a FIB-SEM microscope can collect synapse-ready images much faster than before.

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM is the only method with resolution to reconstruct dense neural morphology, but even modest circuits are too large to trace by hand, so automated instance segmentation is required.
ocar.challenge: Prior pipelines split scarce training data between voxel predictors and agglomeration classifiers, and struggled to serve both nearly isotropic block-face EM and anisotropic serial-section EM at large scale.
ocar.action: Funke, Tschopp, Grisaitis, Sheridan, Singh, Saalfeld and Turaga, in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (2019), train a 3D U-Net to predict voxel affinities with an extended MALIS structured loss, then agglomerate with a learning-free percentile scheme.
ocar.resolution: A quasi-linear MALIS gradient and a two-pass computation avoid early spurious gradients. Simple agglomeration then beats more involved methods on better affinities. On three diverse EM datasets they report relative improvements of 27, 15, and 250 percent, with runtime linear in volume at about 2.6 seconds per megavoxel.
ocar.future_work: Correct parallelization of hierarchical agglomeration still needs research; naive block-wise agglomeration plus overlap stitching was already ‘very satisfying’ on FIB-25.

summaries.beginner: Mapping neurons in electron-microscope volumes means deciding which voxels belong to which cell. This paper trains a 3D neural net to score how voxels should stick together, then groups them with a simple rule, and reports large accuracy gains on several datasets.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TPAMI (2019), Funke, Tschopp and colleagues combine a 3D U-Net for voxel affinities with iterative region agglomeration. Training uses a MALIS-based structured loss that penalizes topological errors after affinity thresholding; they speed the gradient from quadratic to quasi-linear and compute it in two passes. Affinities are accurate enough that learning-free percentile agglomeration outperforms earlier learned agglomerators. Relative improvements of 27, 15, and 250 percent are reported on three EM datasets spanning block-face and serial-section data, at about 2.6 seconds per megavoxel.
summaries.advanced: Which dataset corresponds to which percentage is not named in the selected text. ‘State of the art’ is the authors’ claim against contemporaneous methods. Only the U-Net is trained, which they treat as an advantage, but agglomeration quality then rides entirely on affinity quality. Hierarchical agglomeration is linear yet nontrivial to parallelize correctly.

plain_language_summary: Mapping neurons in electron-microscope volumes means deciding which voxels belong to which cell. This paper trains a 3D neural net to score how voxels should stick together, then groups them with a simple rule, and reports large accuracy gains on several datasets.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput EM now reconstructs mammalian circuits at synaptic resolution, so it is possible to ask how the physical size of a synapse relates to how strongly it transmits.
ocar.challenge: Without that structure–function link, wiring diagrams cannot be given physiological weights. Whether neocortical synapses use one or many release sites was also unsettled.
ocar.action: Holler, Köstinger, Martin, Schuhknecht and Stratford, in Nature, combine slice electrophysiology of synaptically connected pyramidal neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex with correlated light microscopy and high-resolution EM of all putative contacts between the recorded cells.
ocar.resolution: Synapse size and strength are linearly related, supplying a missing conversion from EM morphology to weight. Quantal analysis indicates at least 2.7 neurotransmitter-release sites on average, supporting multivesicular release and a more complex view of cortical synapses.
ocar.future_work: The implied next use is to assign physiological weights to synapses in EM connectomes and to treat neocortical synapses as computational devices with multiple release sites.

summaries.beginner: Connectomes show which nerve cells touch, but not how strong each contact is. This study records from connected mouse cortical cells and then images those same synapses, finding that bigger contacts are stronger and that each synapse likely has several release sites.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature, Holler, Köstinger, Martin, Schuhknecht and Stratford paired slice physiology of connected pyramidal neurons in mouse somatosensory cortex with correlated light and electron microscopy of all putative contacts. They report a linear relationship between synapse size and transmission strength. Quantal analysis indicates at least 2.7 release sites on average, challenging single-site release models and supporting multivesicular release. The result is framed as the missing link for weighting EM-reconstructed synapses.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF extract is not this article, so this card uses the catalog abstract only. Organism tags on the catalog row list C. elegans; the study is mouse neocortex. ‘At least 2.7’ is an average lower bound from quantal analysis, not a count per synapse in every cell. Linearity is reported for the measured pairs, not proven for all cortical synapse types.

plain_language_summary: Connectomes show which nerve cells touch, but not how strong each contact is. This study records from connected mouse cortical cells and then images those same synapses, finding that bigger contacts are stronger and that each synapse likely has several release sites.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM connectomics aims to recover every synaptic connection. Cleft detection is comparatively mature; the remaining step is to name the pre- and postsynaptic cells at each cleft.
ocar.challenge: Most machine-learning methods treat partner assignment as classification of candidate cell pairs, which requires proposing partners and does not directly paint the partner voxels.
ocar.action: Turner, Lee, Lu, Wu, Ih and Seung, in the IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging (2019), train a convolutional net that takes local image context plus a binary cleft mask and outputs two masks: presynaptic and postsynaptic partner voxels. The cleft acts as an attentional gate.
ocar.resolution: They report that an implementation performs well on mouse somatosensory cortex and evaluate it inside a combined system that predicts both clefts and connections.
ocar.future_work: The extract does not give a named production volume or error tables; applying the same attentional assignment to larger, more anisotropic volumes is the natural next test.

summaries.beginner: After a synapse’s gap is found in an electron-microscope image, a computer still has to say which two cells meet there. This paper trains a network that, given the gap, paints the voxels of the sending and receiving partners.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE ISBI (2019), Turner, Lee, Lu, Wu, Ih and Seung reframe synaptic partner assignment as mask generation rather than candidate classification. A convolutional network receives image context and a single cleft mask and is trained to emit presynaptic and postsynaptic voxel masks, with the cleft as an attentional gating signal. They test on mouse somatosensory cortex and fold the method into a combined cleft-plus-connection predictor. Visual cues discussed include vesicles, clefts, and dendritic spines with spine apparatus.
summaries.advanced: No numeric precision or recall appears in the selected text; ‘performs well’ is the authors’ qualitative report. The method assumes a cleft is already localized. Evaluation is on one cortical dataset; generalization to insect polyadic synapses is not demonstrated here.

plain_language_summary: After a synapse’s gap is found in an electron-microscope image, a computer still has to say which two cells meet there. This paper trains a network that, given the gap, paints the voxels of the sending and receiving partners.

ocar.opportunity: Deep convolutional nets now make automated neuron and organelle segmentation accurate enough for micro-connectomics, including U-Net variants and flood-filling networks.
ocar.challenge: Existing CNN pipelines require Python, framework knowledge, ground-truth preparation, and data conversion, which blocks non-experts and even many computer-literate biologists.
ocar.action: Urakubo, Bullmann, Kubota, Oba and Ishii, in Scientific Reports (2019), present UNI-EM, a desktop collection covering ground truth, training, inference, postprocessing, proofreading, and visualization, wrapping 2D CNNs (U-Net, ResNet, HighwayNet, DenseNet) and 3D flood-filling networks.
ocar.resolution: Example workflows cover mitochondria with a 2D CNN and neurons with FFNs. Test users without Python completed the procedures; the authors report accuracies comparable to contemporary methods, with mitochondria extracted in 2 hours at higher accuracy than AdaBoost.
ocar.future_work: They position UNI-EM as a testing platform before committing to professional large-scale segmentation. GPU training is desktop-bound; remote users get proofreading and TensorBoard only.

summaries.beginner: Cutting-edge neuron-tracing networks are usually locked behind Python and specialist software. UNI-EM packages those tools into a desktop environment so biologists can train and check segmentations without writing code.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2019), Urakubo, Bullmann, Kubota, Oba and Ishii describe UNI-EM for 2D and 3D CNN-based EM segmentation. It unifies annotation, training, inference, postprocessing, proofreading (including Dojo), and visualization, bundling U-Net, ResNet, HighwayNet, DenseNet, and wrapped flood-filling networks. Two tutorials—mitochondria via 2D CNN and neurons via FFNs—let non-programmers run the stack. Test users succeeded, with mitochondria work in 2 hours beating AdaBoost in the authors’ comparison.
summaries.advanced: ‘State-of-the-art level’ refers to the wrapped published architectures, not a new accuracy record from UNI-EM itself. Only a desktop user can submit GPU training jobs. 2D CNNs plus z-stitching are said to suffice for simple shapes such as mitochondria; neuron segmentation still wants strong 3D methods or high-performance z-connectors.

plain_language_summary: Cutting-edge neuron-tracing networks are usually locked behind Python and specialist software. UNI-EM packages those tools into a desktop environment so biologists can train and check segmentations without writing code.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans is small enough that complete, quantitative wiring from sense organs to muscles can be written down for both adult sexes, giving a basis to model behavior.
ocar.challenge: Earlier maps were incomplete, especially the male head, and did not systematically compare sexes. Connectivity is only part of communication; extrasynaptic signals also matter.
ocar.action: Cook, Jarrell, Brittin, Wang, Bloniarz, Yakovlev, Nguyen, Tang, Bayer, Duerr, Bülow, Hobert, Hall and Emmons, in Nature (2019), update serial-EM reconstructions from new and published micrographs and compile whole-animal connectivity matrices for hermaphrodite and male, with fluorescent checks of synapses.
ocar.resolution: Nervous systems differ between sexes at multiple levels: dimorphic structure and connectivity of some sex-shared neurons, sex-specific inputs into central circuits, and many shared connections that differ in strength. Data are released at wormwiring.org.
ocar.future_work: They treat the maps as conceptualizations built from multiple animals, including inferred repeated connections, and as snapshots of a dynamic structure. Modeling should use synapse placement, not only the adjacency matrix, and should include extrasynaptic transmission.

summaries.beginner: The roundworm C. elegans has a tiny nervous system that can be mapped cell by cell in both sexes. This paper updates those maps and shows that males and hermaphrodites share many cells but wire them differently.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2019), Cook, Jarrell, Hall, Emmons and colleagues present quantitative whole-animal connectomes for adult hermaphrodite and male C. elegans, spanning sensory input to end organs. Serial EM of new and published series, including the male head, is combined with fluorescent synapse labeling. Sex-shared neurons used in sexual behavior can be dimorphic; sex-specific circuitry feeds into central pathways; many shared edges differ in strength. Matrices are intended as starting points for modeling behavior.
summaries.advanced: Maps are stitched across animals and include some connections assumed from serial repetition or seen only in the opposite sex. Individual worms will differ; larval outgrowth and experience-dependent change continue into adulthood. High convergence onto motor neurons defies simple pathway reading. Structural connectomes omit extrasynaptic transmitter, peptide, and hormone signaling.

plain_language_summary: The roundworm C. elegans has a tiny nervous system that can be mapped cell by cell in both sexes. This paper updates those maps and shows that males and hermaphrodites share many cells but wire them differently.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM can now map new C. elegans connectomes faster and with less subjectivity than White et al.’s fully manual 1986 reconstruction, and can include associated non-neuronal tissues.
ocar.challenge: Gaps remain in the original map. Open questions include development, individuality, sexual dimorphism, and genetic or environmental regulation of connectivity. Annotator variability still needs control.
ocar.action: Mulcahy, Witvliet, Holmyard, Mitchell, Chisholm, Meirovitch, Samuel and Zhen, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), describe their current vEM pipeline for the worm nervous system, including high-pressure freezing, and sketch projected improvements.
ocar.resolution: The paper is a methods account rather than a new complete connectome. They advise acquiring connectomes from multiple animals to separate annotator noise from biology, and note that the same volumes capture skin, gut, muscle, excretory, and reproductive ultrastructure.
ocar.future_work: Projected pipeline improvements for C. elegans and other systems, and reuse of the volumes by cell biologists beyond neuroscience.

summaries.beginner: The first complete wiring diagram of an animal was traced by hand in a tiny worm decades ago. This methods paper explains a modern volume-electron-microscopy pipeline for making new worm maps faster and for asking how wiring changes with age, sex, and experience.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), Mulcahy, Witvliet, Samuel, Zhen and colleagues review why C. elegans remains a connectomics workhorse and describe their volume EM pipeline. After White et al. (1986), newer vEM aims to fill remaining gaps and to study development, individuality, sexual dimorphism, and gene–environment effects on connectivity. High-pressure freezing is among the methods discussed. They recommend multiple animals to bound annotator variability.
summaries.advanced: This is a pipeline description, not a release of a new whole-animal matrix. Throughput and ‘reduced subjectivity’ are goals of current vEM, not quantified here as a single error rate. Non-neuronal tissues are captured but not analyzed in this paper.

plain_language_summary: The first complete wiring diagram of an animal was traced by hand in a tiny worm decades ago. This methods paper explains a modern volume-electron-microscopy pipeline for making new worm maps faster and for asking how wiring changes with age, sex, and experience.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic reconstruction from EM stacks is a demanding multi-object tracking problem: many intertwined neurites must be followed with pixel accuracy across slices.
ocar.challenge: Iterated single-object trackers such as flood-filling networks repeat redundant computation and, at the accuracy that currently leads, need computing infrastructure most laboratories cannot afford.
ocar.action: Meirovitch, Mi, Saribekyan, Matveev, Rolnick and Shavit, at CVPR (2019), introduce cross-classification clustering (3C): a logarithmic number of independent per-image classifications whose cross-labels uniquely assign each pixel to an object.
ocar.resolution: They report state-of-the-art connectomics accuracy and an order-of-magnitude scalability gain over existing single-object tracking, aiming to bring high-quality reconstruction within reach of more labs.
ocar.future_work: They suggest the same encoding may help video segmentation and medical imagery.

summaries.beginner: Following every nerve fiber through a stack of microscope images usually means chasing one cell at a time. This computer-vision paper instead classifies all cells at once with a clever combination of a few labels, which is much cheaper to compute.
summaries.intermediate: At CVPR (2019), Meirovitch, Mi, Saribekyan, Matveev, Rolnick and Shavit present cross-classification clustering (3C) for 3D instance segmentation in connectomics. Instead of iterated single-object tracking or segment-then-match, they run a logarithmic number of independent classifications per image; the cross-product of labels identifies instances. Applied to EM volumes, they claim state-of-the-art accuracy and roughly ten-fold better scalability than flood-filling networks. The motivation is that leading methods currently demand computing beyond most laboratories.
summaries.advanced: ‘State-of-the-art’ and ‘order of magnitude’ are author claims in the abstract; the selected extract does not tabulate error-free path length against FFN. Benefits for video and medical imaging are proposed, not shown. Casimir Wierzynski is listed among catalog authors but not on the arXiv author line in the extract.

plain_language_summary: Following every nerve fiber through a stack of microscope images usually means chasing one cell at a time. This computer-vision paper instead classifies all cells at once with a clever combination of a few labels, which is much cheaper to compute.

ocar.opportunity: 3D EM can image every cell and chemical synapse in a piece of cortex, but dense reconstruction—not imaging—has been the bottleneck, limiting prior dense cortical maps to femtoliter-scale volumes.
ocar.challenge: Automated segmentations remain too error-prone to use as-is, so human–machine analysis efficiency determines progress. Geometric models also may not predict cortical wiring.
ocar.action: Motta, Berning, Boergens, Staffler, Beining, Loomba, Schramm, Hennig, Wissler and Helmstaedter, in Science, raise automated segmentation quality, route humans only to likely errors, and optimize in-browser ‘data flight,’ reconstructing layer 4 of mouse barrel cortex.
ocar.resolution: They densely reconstruct about 500,000 cubic micrometers and 2.7 m of cable in about 4,000 human hours—about 300 times larger than previous dense cortical reconstructions, at about 20-fold higher efficiency. A connectome among neurites with at least 10 synapses each comprises 153,171 synapses. Inhibitory axon types show subcellular target specificity; beyond about 5 μm, geometry poorly predicts the circuit. They also bound the fraction of synapses consistent with saturated long-term potentiation.
ocar.future_work: The approach is offered for connectomic phenotyping across cortices, layers, species, ages, sensory experience, and disease.

summaries.beginner: Mammalian cortex is packed so tightly that mapping every wire and synapse in even a small block has been nearly impossible. This study reconstructs a much larger piece of mouse barrel cortex than before and reads cell types and possible learning traces from the wiring alone.
summaries.intermediate: In Science, Motta, Helmstaedter and colleagues densely reconstruct about 500,000 cubic micrometers of layer 4 mouse somatosensory (barrel) cortex—about 300 times larger than earlier dense cortical maps—using improved automation plus targeted human proofreading (about 4,000 hours; problems solved in about 29 seconds each). They report 2.7 m of cable and a connectome of 153,171 synapses among 6,979 pre- and 3,719 postsynaptic neurites with at least 10 synapses. Connectomic data defined inhibitory axon types with subcellular specificity; coarser random-wiring models were rejected. A thalamocortical synapse-density gradient and upper bounds on a Hebbian ‘learned’ fraction are described.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF extract is not this article, so numbers follow the catalog abstract. The short summary’s ‘89 neurons’ is a morphological subset, not the full neurite census (figure caption: 34,221 axons and 11,400 postsynaptic processes; ~400,000 synapses). ‘Learnedness’ is an upper bound on synapses consistent with saturated LTP, not a measured learning experiment. Catalog year is 2018; the Science article of this DOI appeared in 2019.

plain_language_summary: Mammalian cortex is packed so tightly that mapping every wire and synapse in even a small block has been nearly impossible. This study reconstructs a much larger piece of mouse barrel cortex than before and reads cell types and possible learning traces from the wiring alone.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section array tomography, serial block-face imaging, and FIB-SEM already give three-dimensional EM, and multi-beam SEM plus automated preparation robots now make cubic-millimeter, high-resolution mapping plausible.
ocar.challenge: Standard single-beam scanning is too slow, so most volume-EM studies are restricted to relatively small tissue volumes.
ocar.action: Eberle and Zeidler, in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2018), mini-review volume EM approaches with emphasis on serial-section array tomography and multi-beam scanning electron microscopy developed for large-area imaging.
ocar.resolution: They argue that mapping cubic-millimeter-range volumes at high resolution is now within reach when multi-beam SEM is paired with commercial sample-preparation robots.
ocar.future_work: Integrate storage and compute with the microscope; improve stage precision and move times; raise contrast so fewer electrons per pixel suffice; adopt faster ablation such as high-speed ion milling; put existing machine-learning tracers into scalable architectures.

summaries.beginner: Scanning electron microscopes usually look at one tiny patch at a time, which makes big brain volumes slow to image. This short review explains multi-beam SEM and related volume methods that are meant to photograph much larger pieces of tissue.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2018), Eberle and Zeidler (Carl Zeiss Microscopy) survey 3D EM for connectomics: array tomography, serial block-face imaging, and FIB tomography, then focus on multi-beam SEM built for large sample areas. They note that throughput, not the idea of volume EM, has limited mapped size. With automated preparation robots, they judge cubic-millimeter high-resolution mapping to be within reach. Outlook items include tighter stage control, higher contrast for faster scans, and scalable compute.
summaries.advanced: This is an industry mini-review, not a new connectome. ‘Within reach’ is a capability claim, not a completed mm³ reconstruction in this paper. Funding is from Carl Zeiss Microscopy GmbH. In vivo methods (DTI, fMRI) are discussed only to note that they do not reveal synaptic connections.

plain_language_summary: Scanning electron microscopes usually look at one tiny patch at a time, which makes big brain volumes slow to image. This short review explains multi-beam SEM and related volume methods that are meant to photograph much larger pieces of tissue.

ocar.opportunity: Modern EM volumes are multi-terabyte, many segments are mostly correct, and individual bodies can be several gigavoxels, while several proofreaders must work at once.
ocar.challenge: Older tools expected datasets to be split into subsets and did not offer low-latency 3D views of huge mutable segments, interactive splits of giant false merges, or lock-based collaboration.
ocar.action: Zhao, Olbris, Yu and Plaza, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), introduce NeuTu as a DVID client with fast 3D visualization, optimized semi-automatic split of false merges, bookmarking, proofreading history, and real-time locks.
ocar.resolution: They proofread fly medulla (~11,491 neurons; ~53,500 pre- and ~315,500 postsynaptic sites in the reported table) and mushroom body (983 neurons; 89,406 pre- and 224,697 postsynaptic sites) without partitioning the volume. Downsampling to scale 5 yields 109 ± 66 ms 3D conversion; 3D visualization roughly doubled productivity on false splits. Seven neurons were added to NeuroMorpho.
ocar.future_work: Loading hundreds of large bodies can exhaust memory; they suggest skeleton views and tighter data structures. Later stages need biological queries, synapse-size annotation, and subcellular detail.

summaries.beginner: After a computer carves an electron-microscope volume into candidate neurons, people still have to fix mistakes in objects that can be enormous. NeuTu is a collaborative 3D editor, built on the DVID database, for doing that on whole fly-brain datasets.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), Zhao, Olbris, Yu and Plaza present NeuTu for proofreading high-quality segmentations in multi-terabyte EM. As a DVID client it offers low-latency 3D views of mutable bodies, interactive splitting of gigavoxel false merges, history, and lock-based simultaneous editing so volumes need not be split among users. It supported fly medulla and mushroom-body connectomes an order of magnitude more complex, by connection count, than prior maps they cite. 3D visualization at downsample scale 5 responded in 109 ± 66 ms and roughly doubled false-split productivity.
summaries.advanced: Neuron counts include unidentified segments and therefore exceed some earlier 7-column papers. ‘Order of magnitude more complex’ is the authors’ comparison by connection number. Memory blow-ups when loading many large bodies remain. Catalog organism is empty; the worked examples are Drosophila.

plain_language_summary: After a computer carves an electron-microscope volume into candidate neurons, people still have to fix mistakes in objects that can be enormous. NeuTu is a collaborative 3D editor, built on the DVID database, for doing that on whole fly-brain datasets.

ocar.opportunity: Dense synaptic reconstruction in model brains is now technologically feasible, analogous to genomics a generation earlier. Drosophila has manageable cell numbers and genetically identifiable neuron classes.
ocar.challenge: Human proofreading of segmented bodies remains the slowest step. Most neurites are both pre- and postsynaptic, and each site has multiple postsynaptic partners, so pathway strength must be interpreted carefully.
ocar.action: Meinertzhagen, in Journal of Experimental Biology (2018), offers a personal perspective on Drosophila connectomics driven by FIB-SEM, image alignment, and computer-aided morphology, distinguishing major pathways (100 or more presynaptic contacts) from minor ones (fewer than about 10).
ocar.resolution: He expects a complete adult fly connectome within a few years of writing, with the larva possibly sooner. The scientific payoff is causal tests—silencing or activating identified neurons—and discovery of unsuspected pathways that predict new behaviors.
ocar.future_work: Connectomes should explain behavioral differences among brains, support evolutionary comparison of circuits, and eventually inform vertebrate strategies and cognitive disorders with a connectomic basis.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies are small enough that every synapse in the brain can, in principle, be listed. This essay argues why that list is worth the remaining proofreading grind: it lets us turn identified cells on and off and watch behavior change.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Experimental Biology (2018), Meinertzhagen reviews a decade of dense Drosophila circuit reconstruction, especially via FIB-SEM. He separates major pathways (100 or more presynaptic contacts) from minor ones (fewer than about 10) and notes that neurites are typically both pre- and postsynaptic at polyadic sites. He forecasts a complete adult connectome within a few years and a larval one possibly sooner, with proofreading still rate-limiting. The use-case is causal circuit-to-behavior experiments and finding unexpected pathways.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF extract is not this article, so this card uses the catalog abstract. Forecasts of ‘a few years’ are from 2018. The 100-versus-10 contact threshold is a heuristic, not a physiological cutoff. Catalog method tags list FIB-SEM and a larval dataset; the essay also discusses adult work.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies are small enough that every synapse in the brain can, in principle, be listed. This essay argues why that list is worth the remaining proofreading grind: it lets us turn identified cells on and off and watch behavior change.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM can in principle annotate every synapse as well as every neurite. Automatic synapse detection already works well on near-isotropic vertebrate EM.
ocar.challenge: On highly anisotropic insect serial-section TEM, results had not matched human annotation. Synapses are sparse, and FAFB-scale volumes are tens of tera-voxels.
ocar.action: Heinrich, Funke, Pape, Nunez-Iglesias and Saalfeld, at MICCAI (2018), design a 3D U-Net with isotropic fields of view on non-isotropic data, train by regression on a signed distance transform of CREMI synaptic clefts, and run parallel prediction on the full adult fly brain.
ocar.resolution: They report a significant improvement over prior methods with fewer parameters than a previous architecture. About 50 tera-voxels of biological sample (of ~213 tera-voxels including background) were predicted in less than five days at about 3 megavoxels per second per GPU across 48 GPUs. Predictions generalize far from the CREMI training region, including lamina, and visually match nc82 synaptic-density patterns.
ocar.future_work: Code is released as open source. The conclusion emphasizes the architectural and engineering result rather than a named error-rate target for later versions.

summaries.beginner: Finding every synapse in a fruit-fly brain imaged as thin, stretched slices is harder than in cube-shaped vertebrate volumes. This paper trains a 3D network on the shape of synaptic clefts and runs it over an entire adult fly brain in days.
summaries.intermediate: At MICCAI (2018), Heinrich, Funke, Pape, Nunez-Iglesias and Saalfeld target synaptic clefts in anisotropic ssTEM of Drosophila. A 3D U-Net is shaped for isotropic fields of view in non-isotropic data and trained by regression on signed distance transforms of CREMI cleft annotations. Using N5 + Dask on 48 GPUs, they predict the masked FAFB sample (~50 tera-voxels) in under five days at ~3 megavoxels s⁻¹ GPU⁻¹. Quality is described as consistent with CREMI, including in lamina, with an nc82-like projection matching a template brain.
summaries.advanced: ‘Significant improvement over the state of the art’ is not accompanied in the extract by a single precision/recall number. Visual nc82 comparison is across unregistered individuals. FIB-SEM is cited at ‘~53 nm’ in the introduction, which conflicts with common 8 nm FIB-SEM figures and may be a typesetting issue; the method itself is for ssTEM. Training is on CREMI, not on every fly neuropil type.

plain_language_summary: Finding every synapse in a fruit-fly brain imaged as thin, stretched slices is harder than in cube-shaped vertebrate volumes. This paper trains a 3D network on the shape of synaptic clefts and runs it over an entire adult fly brain in days.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section EM now produces very large, even petabyte-scale, image stacks that scientists need to explore, manually label, and proofread.
ocar.challenge: Software must paint voxels in huge volumes in real time. Many tools cannot stack multiple image and segmentation layers or use one layer as a mask for another.
ocar.action: Berger, Seung and Lichtman, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), introduce VAST (Volume Annotation and Segmentation Tool), a freely available standalone program for annotation and segmentation of large volumetric datasets.
ocar.resolution: VAST supports interactive exploration, efficient manual ground truth, sparse tracing aided by automatic segmentation, and proofreading via trans-layer masking and 3D filling so users inherit accurate outlines from an imperfect automatic segmentation.
ocar.future_work: It is single-user with local segmentation files, so multi-annotator merge is slow. Native skeletons and meshes are absent. A future server-hosted segmentation layer with provenance is proposed.

summaries.beginner: Giant electron-microscope stacks are useless if you cannot paint and correct labels inside them. VAST is a relatively simple desktop tool for coloring cells in very large 3D images, including using a computer’s draft segmentation as a stencil.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), Berger, Seung and Lichtman present VAST for real-time annotation of large voxel volumes, described as usable even in the petabyte range. Typical uses are exploration of EM and light-microscopy stacks, painting training data, sparse volumetric tracing, and proofreading automatic segmentations. Multiple image and segmentation layers can be loaded; trans-layer masking and 3D filling let an automatic segmentation supply outlines while the user assigns identity. It is compared with tools such as TrakEM2 in the keyword list.
summaries.advanced: ‘Petabyte range’ is a capability claim, not a worked example size in the extract. VAST is not a multi-user client–server system; combining users means merging files. Length, diameter, and branching measurements are external. No new biological dataset is released with the paper.

plain_language_summary: Giant electron-microscope stacks are useless if you cannot paint and correct labels inside them. VAST is a relatively simple desktop tool for coloring cells in very large 3D images, including using a computer’s draft segmentation as a stencil.

ocar.opportunity: Leech ganglia are homologous from animal to animal, so an EM volume of one ganglion can be checked against physiology in another, pairing connectomics with functional tests.
ocar.challenge: Physiological connectivity is hard to census at large scale, and light-level overlap does not prove synapses. Some reported physiological connections may lack anatomical contacts.
ocar.action: Pipkin, Bushong, Ellisman and Kristan, in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2018), collect serial block-face EM of an entire juvenile leech ganglion, reconstruct swim-related motor neurons, then reconstruct an uncharacterized pair and record it in an adult ganglion.
ocar.resolution: Known inhibitory motor connections (DI-1 and DI-102 onto DE-3; VI-2 onto VE-4) are confirmed anatomically, with multiple contacts (from 2 to 18 in the examples given) spread across arbor overlap. Some physiological connections were absent in the volume. A newly found anatomical synapse was physiologically functional in the adult.
ocar.future_work: Unexpected extra contacts might be weak, juvenile-only, tracing errors, or gap junctions mistaken for chemical synapses. Other leech subcircuits are better suited to relating contact number to strength.

summaries.beginner: Leeches have repeating packets of identified neurons whose connections were first mapped with electrodes. This study images a whole ganglion in the electron microscope, checks those old connections, and uses the map to find a new synapse that still works when recorded in another animal.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2018), Pipkin, Bushong, Ellisman and Kristan acquire SBEM of an entire juvenile leech ganglion and reconstruct a well-known swim motor circuit. They confirm distributed, multiple chemical contacts between connected motor pairs and report contact counts from 2 (right VI-2 onto left VE-4) to 18 (right DI-1 onto right DE-3). Some connections known from physiology were not found anatomically. An uncharacterized neuron plus a presynaptic partner from the volume yielded a working synapse in adult intracellular recordings.
summaries.advanced: SBEM cannot measure synaptic strength. Juvenile tissue may still be refining synapses. Homology across animals is assumed when physiology is done in a different adult. Catalog metadata list empty organism and SBF-SEM; the animal is leech. Unexpected connections have several non-exclusive explanations listed by the authors.

plain_language_summary: Leeches have repeating packets of identified neurons whose connections were first mapped with electrodes. This study images a whole ganglion in the electron microscope, checks those old connections, and uses the map to find a new synapse that still works when recorded in another animal.

ocar.opportunity: The adult Drosophila brain has on the order of 100,000 neurons and rich behavior, making whole-brain synaptic mapping tractable if imaging can scale. Only EM gives complete, unbiased connectivity.
ocar.challenge: The fly brain is too large for conventional EM platforms. Light-level maps of mushroom-body input clustering may be misleading.
ocar.action: Zheng, Lauritzen, Perlman, Robinson, Nichols, Milkie, Torrens, Price, Fisher, Sharifi, Calle-Schuler, Kmecova, Ali, Karsh, Trautman, Bogovic, Hanslovsky, Jefferis, Kazhdan, Khairy, Saalfeld, Fetter and Bock, in Cell (2018), build a custom high-throughput EM platform and image an entire adult female brain (FAFB), then trace mushroom-body circuitry to validate it.
ocar.resolution: They map the complete set of olfactory inputs to the mushroom body, identify a new calyx input type (MB-CP2) that integrates several sensory modalities, find neurons postsynaptic to Kenyon-cell dendrites, and show that axonal arbors in calyx cluster more tightly than light-level data suggested. Primary postsynaptic targets of Kenyon cells in the MB include other Kenyon cells and the APL neuron. The volume is public.
ocar.future_work: A software pipeline matches EM skeletons to light-microscopy neuron databases to identify cell types and driver lines. The resource is intended to accelerate Drosophila circuit work generally.

summaries.beginner: A fruit-fly brain is small enough to photograph entirely in the electron microscope, but that had not been done. This paper releases that whole-brain volume and uses the mushroom body—the fly’s learning center—to show that new cell types and tighter input clusters appear once synapses are visible.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell (2018), Zheng, Lauritzen, Bock and colleagues image a complete adult female Drosophila brain with a custom high-throughput EM platform and publicly release the volume. Validation traces brain-spanning mushroom-body (MB) circuits: all olfactory inputs to MB calyx, a new multimodal input type MB-CP2, postsynaptic partners of Kenyon-cell dendrites, and tighter clustering of input arbors than in light microscopy. Recurrent microcircuits in calyx include Kenyon cells targeting other Kenyon cells and APL. EM skeletons can be searched against existing light-level morphology databases.
summaries.advanced: This is an imaging resource plus focused MB reconstruction, not a complete whole-brain connectome. The ‘100,000-neuron’ figure is the authors’ scale for the species, not a count of reconstructed cells in this volume. Catalog year is 2017; the Cell paper is 2018. Patent language notes possible financial interest for the corresponding author if licensed.

plain_language_summary: A fruit-fly brain is small enough to photograph entirely in the electron microscope, but that had not been done. This paper releases that whole-brain volume and uses the mushroom body—the fly’s learning center—to show that new cell types and tighter input clusters appear once synapses are visible.

ocar.opportunity: The mushroom body is the insect site of associative learning, where sensory Kenyon cells converge with reinforcement. A synaptic-resolution map of that convergence would constrain models of memory.
ocar.challenge: No comprehensive synaptic description of such a site existed for an animal as complex as Drosophila. Sparse tracing can miss rare cells and cannot support statistics about absent connections.
ocar.action: Takemura, Aso, Hige, Wong, Lu, Xu, Rivlin, Hess, Zhao, Parag, Berg, Huang, Katz, Olbris, Plaza, Umayam and colleagues, in eLife (2017), reconstruct all 983 neurons in the three compartments of the adult MB α lobe from isotropic 8 nm FIB-SEM.
ocar.resolution: Each Kenyon cell makes multiple en passant synapses onto mushroom-body output neurons (MBONs) in a compartment; some MBONs sample all KCs, others are modality-biased. Only 6% of KC→MBON synapses receive a direct dopaminergic (DAN) synapse. Unanticipated classes include KC→DAN and DAN→MBON; DAN activation slowly depolarizes the MBON and can weaken memory recall.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue the dense map enables modeling and experiments that 30 years of MB work did not anticipate, and that sparse tracing would have struggled to prove completeness or the absence of rings and chains.

summaries.beginner: Flies store associations in a brain region called the mushroom body. This paper traces every neuron in part of that region and finds extra synapse types—including from teaching cells straight onto output cells—that textbooks had not drawn.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2017), Takemura, Aso, Rubin, Scheffer and colleagues reconstruct all 983 neurons of the three adult Drosophila mushroom-body α-lobe compartments from 8 nm isotropic FIB-SEM. Kenyon cells, which sparsely encode sensory input, make multiple en passant synapses onto MBONs; MBON sampling of KCs can be complete or modality-specific. Only 6% of KC→MBON synapses are directly contacted by a DAN. They report KC→DAN and DAN→MBON synapses; DAN stimulation slowly depolarizes MBONs and can weaken recall. A rare SIFamide neuron is among cells a sparse strategy might miss.
summaries.advanced: The volume is the α lobe, not the whole mushroom body. ‘Unanticipated’ is relative to prior anatomy and theory, not a claim that no physiological hint existed. The 6% figure is a synapse-level fraction, not a cell-level one. Physiology of DAN→MBON is linked to the anatomical motif but is not a full behavioral dissection in this extract.

plain_language_summary: Flies store associations in a brain region called the mushroom body. This paper traces every neuron in part of that region and finds extra synapse types—including from teaching cells straight onto output cells—that textbooks had not drawn.

ocar.opportunity: Convolutional nets now detect neuronal boundaries well enough that the remaining problem is to find and fix residual split and merge errors in 3D EM segmentations.
ocar.challenge: A typical segmentation has both splits and merges, but prior detectors often handled merges only. Full error-correction nets are expensive if run everywhere.
ocar.action: Zung, Tartavull, Lee and Seung, at NeurIPS (2017), train multiscale 3D convolutional networks for (i) mapping split and merge errors in a candidate object and (ii) object-mask pruning that assumes the candidate is a superset of the true object.
ocar.resolution: The detector reaches high accuracy and can work from shape priors even without the raw image. Feeding the detector’s ‘advice’ (union of erroneous objects) into the corrector improves segmentation over baseline. On a 2048 × 2048 × 256 volume with one Titan X Pascal, boundary detection, error detection, and correction took 18, 25, and 55 minutes.
ocar.future_work: They propose unlimited synthetic errors by mutilating ground truth, directing human annotation to predicted mistakes, using the detector as a learning signal on unlabeled data, and co-training detector and corrector in an adversarial style.

summaries.beginner: Once a computer has drawn draft neurons in an electron-microscope volume, someone still has to find the remaining cuts and accidental joins. This paper trains networks that both highlight those mistakes and propose a cleaned-up cell shape.
summaries.intermediate: At NeurIPS (2017), Zung, Tartavull, Lee and Seung define error detection (a map of splits and merges on a candidate mask) and error correction as mask pruning given a superset object. Multiscale 3D convnets perform both; the corrector improves when its input mask is the detector’s union of error regions (‘advice’). Detectors exploit neuron-shape priors even without image intensity. Restricting expensive correction to predicted error sites saves compute. Timings on a 2048 × 2048 × 256 volume with one Titan X Pascal are 18, 25, and 55 minutes for boundary detection, detection, and correction.
summaries.advanced: ‘High accuracy’ is not given as a single F1 in the selected text. Mask pruning assumes the candidate contains the true object, so it does not by itself add missing branches. Baseline segmentation is from coauthor Lee; TEM data are from the Allen Institute. IARPA funding and a U.S. Government disclaimer apply.

plain_language_summary: Once a computer has drawn draft neurons in an electron-microscope volume, someone still has to find the remaining cuts and accidental joins. This paper trains networks that both highlight those mistakes and propose a cleaned-up cell shape.

ocar.opportunity: Teravoxel EM volumes can now be acquired in weeks, so automatic conversion of skeleton tracings into a richly annotated synaptic matrix would remove years of manual classification of organelles, synapse types, and cell compartments.
ocar.challenge: Human analysis of such volumes still takes years if mitochondria, synapses, axons, dendrites, spines, myelin, somata, and cell types are labeled by hand.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald, Schubert, Killinger, Urban, Mikula, Svara and Kornfeld, in Nature Methods, present SyConn: deep convolutional nets and random forests that annotate those structures from manual neurite skeletons, tested on serial block-face EM from zebrafish, mouse, and zebra finch, including synaptic wiring of songbird basal ganglia.
ocar.resolution: Basal-ganglia cell types with high in vivo firing rates had higher densities of mitochondria and vesicles. Synapse sizes and quantities scaled systematically with the innervated postsynaptic cell types.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames SyConn as a way to finish annotation once skeletons exist; applying the same stack to additional species and nuclei is the implied extension.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope volumes are now huge, but turning traced cells into a table of synapses, cell parts, and cell types still eats years. SyConn is software that fills in those labels automatically and is used here to read wiring in a songbird brain region.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods, Dorkenwald, Schubert, Svara, Kornfeld and colleagues introduce SyConn, which uses convolutional networks and random forests to infer a richly annotated connectivity matrix from manual neurite skeletons. The classifier suite covers mitochondria, synapses and synapse types, axons, dendrites, spines, myelin, somata, and cell types. Tests use SBF-SEM from zebrafish, mouse, and zebra finch; they compute synaptic wiring of songbird basal ganglia. High-firing cell types showed higher mitochondrial and vesicle densities, and synapse size and number scaled with postsynaptic type.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF extract is not this article, so this card uses the catalog abstract. No numeric precision/recall for SyConn appears there. ‘Teravoxel in weeks versus years of analysis’ is the authors’ scale contrast. Catalog organisms include zebrafish and ‘other’ (songbird).

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope volumes are now huge, but turning traced cells into a table of synapses, cell parts, and cell types still eats years. SyConn is software that fills in those labels automatically and is used here to read wiring in a songbird brain region.

ocar.opportunity: As a Drosophila larva grows, circuits must keep producing appropriate output. Identified nociceptive neurons can be reconstructed in first- and third-instar EM volumes to see how structure tracks growth.
ocar.challenge: Whether morphology and synapse numbers scale so as to preserve computation—for example, localizing a nociceptive stimulus—was unclear.
ocar.action: Gerhard, Andrade, Fetter, Cardona and Schneider-Mizell, in a 2017 bioRxiv preprint, reconstruct an identified nociceptive circuit in one 1st-instar and one 3rd-instar larva using new and existing serial-section EM.
ocar.resolution: Circuit structure is extremely consistent and topographic. Interneurons grow about five-fold in cable and synaptic input, with compensatory changes that keep cell-type-specific input as a fraction of total input. Synapse counts rise with a disproportionate increase in small dendritic terminal branches. Numerically strong mdIV→LN contacts scale almost with total input.
ocar.future_work: They ask whether inhibitory connections follow the same rules, and whether receptor or release properties change alongside structure. The same homeostatic scaling might buffer food restriction or evolutionary size differences (e.g. Calliphora vs Drosophila visual neurons).

summaries.beginner: A maggot’s body grows enormously, yet its nerve cells must keep reporting touch and pain in the right place. This study compares the same identified circuit in a young and an older larva and finds the wiring pattern stays the same even as cells get much larger.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (2017), Gerhard, Andrade, Fetter, Cardona and Schneider-Mizell reconstruct an identified Drosophila nociceptive circuit in 1st- and 3rd-instar serial-section EM volumes. They report highly stereotyped, topographic connectivity. About five-fold growth in interneuron cable and synapse number is accompanied by conservation of each input type’s share of total synapses, plus extra small dendritic twigs. They propose that this structural growth conserves computation such as stimulus location. Strong mdIV→LN connections scale nearly with total input; the weakest connections scale more.
summaries.advanced: Only two animals (one per stage) are compared. Sensory connections emphasized here are excitatory; inhibitory development is explicitly untested. Linear dendritic integration is inferred from adult fly literature, not measured in these larvae. Catalog year matches the preprint; a later journal version may exist.

plain_language_summary: A maggot’s body grows enormously, yet its nerve cells must keep reporting touch and pain in the right place. This study compares the same identified circuit in a young and an older larva and finds the wiring pattern stays the same even as cells get much larger.

ocar.opportunity: HVC in the zebra finch generates precisely timed sequences that pace song. Mapping who HVC(RA) ‘pacer’ axons contact can test synaptic-chain models of that sequence.
ocar.challenge: Pairwise electrical recordings had found very low connection rates, which some took as evidence against a direct chain among HVC(RA) cells. Sequence-generating anatomy was otherwise unknown.
ocar.action: Kornfeld, Benezra, Narayanan, Svara, Egger, Oberlaender, Denk and Long, in eLife (2017), combine serial block-face EM with light microscopy to classify postsynaptic targets of HVC(RA) axons by distance from the soma.
ocar.resolution: Near the soma, axons almost exclusively hit inhibitory interneurons, matching paired recordings. Farther away, targets are mostly other excitatory neurons, about half of them other HVC(RA) cells. They estimate that about 25% of excitatory inputs onto HVC(RA) neurons are homotypic, and that ~200 such inputs among ~40,000 HVC(RA) cells imply at most ~0.5% pairwise connection probability—reconciling sparse physiology with a chain.
ocar.future_work: The remaining ~75% of excitatory inputs (Uva, NIf, HVC(X) collaterals, auditory afferents, etc.) should be quantified at single-cell resolution. Uva’s role is highlighted as unresolved.

summaries.beginner: Songbirds sing with clock-like timing from a brain area called HVC. This study follows the timing cells’ axons in the electron microscope and finds they inhibit neighbors locally but excite other timing cells farther away—wiring that could carry a wave of song.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2017), Kornfeld, Benezra, Denk, Long and colleagues map postsynaptic targets of zebra finch HVC(RA) neurons with SBEM plus light microscopy. Proximal axons almost exclusively contact inhibitory interneurons, consistent with paired physiology. Distal targets are mostly excitatory, about half other HVC(RA) cells. They argue this supports global synaptic chains embedded in local inhibitory networks. Homotypic synapses are estimated at 25% of excitatory input to HVC(RA) cells; ~200 such inputs per cell among ~40,000 HVC(RA) neurons yield at most 0.5% pairwise probability, matching rare paired connections.
summaries.advanced: Which remaining excitatory sources are ‘chain’ synapses is unknown. Some afferents (NIf, auditory) are unlikely to pattern song based on cited lesions, but Uva is unsettled. Cell-type classification uses spine density and morphology; errors there would shift distal excitatory fractions. Sequence generation is inferred from anatomy plus prior physiology, not from singing during the EM experiment.

plain_language_summary: Songbirds sing with clock-like timing from a brain area called HVC. This study follows the timing cells’ axons in the electron microscope and finds they inhibit neighbors locally but excite other timing cells farther away—wiring that could carry a wave of song.

ocar.opportunity: FIB-SEM already offers <10 nm isotropic voxels and easy registration, which helps tracing of thin neurites and reduces proofreading if it can run long enough to cover connectomic volumes.
ocar.challenge: Slow SEM imaging and poor long-term stability had capped contiguous volumes. The method is destructive, so interrupts permanently fragment the dataset.
ocar.action: Xu, Hayworth, Lu, Grob, Hassan, García-Cerdán, Niyogi, Nogales, Weinberg and Hess, in eLife (2017), describe engineering that speeds acquisition and keeps FIB-SEM stable for months.
ocar.resolution: Systems operate for months and collect continuously imaged volumes larger than 10^6 µm³, large enough for connectomics. Higher-resolution (~4 nm isotropic) mode is shown on smaller (5–50 µm linear) volumes. Example datasets include mammalian neuropil, Drosophila brain, and Chlamydomonas.
ocar.future_work: They expect other labs and commercial systems to adopt the enhancements, and they position high-resolution cell-sized volumes as an alternative to stitched serial-section TEM tomography in cell biology.

summaries.beginner: A focused ion beam can shave a sample one thin layer at a time while a scanning electron microscope photographs each new face, giving sharp 3D pictures. This paper shows how to keep that process running for months so the pictures cover volumes useful for tracing neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2017), Xu, Hayworth, Hess and colleagues tackle FIB-SEM’s historic limits—slow imaging and short reliable runs—with techniques that accelerate acquisition and improve stability. They report months of operation and continuously imaged volumes >10^6 µm³, with x, y, and z resolution all <10 nm in the connectomic mode. A higher-resolution (~4 nm isotropic) mode addresses 5–50 µm-scale cell-biology volumes. Demonstrations include mammalian neural tissue, Drosophila brain, and the alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
summaries.advanced: Throughput remains below TEM because SEM is serial, low-energy, and cannot post-stain sections. Destructive milling forbids re-imaging after failures. ‘>10^6 µm³’ is a capability statement, not a named public connectome in this paper. Catalog organism is fly; examples also include mammal and alga.

plain_language_summary: A focused ion beam can shave a sample one thin layer at a time while a scanning electron microscope photographs each new face, giving sharp 3D pictures. This paper shows how to keep that process running for months so the pictures cover volumes useful for tracing neurons.

ocar.opportunity: Reliable circuit diagrams from volume EM require tracing complete cells, including all neurites, with error rates low enough that proofreading does not dominate.
ocar.challenge: Prior automated tracers left too many errors. Methods that generate affinities or boundaries still need a separate clustering stage and do not iteratively reshape a single object.
ocar.action: Januszewski, Kornfeld, Li, Pope, Blakely, Lindsey, Maitin-Shepard, Tyka, Denk and Jain, in Nature Methods (and a 2017 bioRxiv preprint of the same work), introduce flood-filling networks: a convolutional net with a recurrent pathway that iteratively extends one neuronal process, applied to serial block-face EM of zebra finch brain.
ocar.resolution: Mean error-free neurite path length is 1.1 mm, an order of magnitude better than previous published methods on the same dataset. Only four mergers occurred in a 97 mm test set. A roughly 1 million cubic micron volume was segmented. Compute cost is high: about 74 times a baseline CNN, with each voxel processed on average 59 times per run.
ocar.future_work: They argue savings in human split-correction will outweigh compute, and that large segments plus topological checks (must hit a soma or the volume border) can focus remaining proofreading as error-free path length grows.

summaries.beginner: Computers that trace neurons in electron-microscope images usually still make enough mistakes that people spend months fixing them. Flood-filling networks follow one fiber at a time and, in songbird tissue, go more than a millimeter between mistakes.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods, Januszewski, Kornfeld, Denk, Jain and colleagues present flood-filling networks (FFNs): a CNN plus a recurrent pathway that iteratively grows a single neurite. On SBEM of male zebra finch brain they report 1.1 mm mean error-free path length—an order of magnitude above prior published results on the same data—and only four mergers in 97 mm of test neurites. Direct segment generation, single-object inference, and multi-seed ensembling reduce mergers. The pipeline cost about 74× a baseline fully convolutional 3D CNN.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract is the 2017 bioRxiv typesetting of the same study; catalog venue is Nature Methods. Computational cost may dominate in labs without large GPU clusters. Error-free path length is a skeleton metric, not a full synaptic connectome. Merger count is on a neurite test set, not every object in the million-cubic-micron volume.

plain_language_summary: Computers that trace neurons in electron-microscope images usually still make enough mistakes that people spend months fixing them. Flood-filling networks follow one fiber at a time and, in songbird tissue, go more than a millimeter between mistakes.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila now has large light-microscopy datasets, driver lines, activity tools, and 3D EM, so neuronal types and circuits can be characterized at scale and compared with vertebrates.
ocar.challenge: A larval whole-brain connectome was nearing completion by manual EM reconstruction, but an adult brain is about 40 times larger and would take roughly 500–5,000 person-years if done the same way. Light, EM, and physiology still live in separate resources.
ocar.action: Schlegel, Costa and Jefferis, in Current Opinion in Insect Science (2017), review available Drosophila data and tools and the prospects for integrating them.
ocar.resolution: They report that an adult whole-brain EM dataset is already public with focused reconstruction underway, and that rapid gains in imaging and especially automated segmentation will likely yield a complete adult connectome within about five years of their writing.
ocar.future_work: They call for databases that combine light and EM with functional measurements, and they discuss how the same path could extend to larger insects and vertebrates.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly neuroscience suddenly has both genetic remote controls and electron-microscope wiring diagrams. This review asks how to put those maps together—and how long a full adult-brain connectome will take if computers, not only people, do the tracing.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Insect Science (2017), Schlegel, Costa and Jefferis survey Drosophila resources: large light-level datasets, driver lines, activity reporters, and 3D EM. A larval whole-brain connectome was approaching completion by manual reconstruction. The adult volume, about 40 times larger, would require ~500–5,000 person-years of manual labor, but a public adult dataset already supported focused reconstruction. They predict automated segmentation will deliver a complete adult connectome within five years. Integration with physiology is presented as essential to explain behavior.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF extract is not this article, so this card uses the catalog abstract. The five-year forecast is from 2017. Person-year ranges depend on assumed reconstruction speed. Catalog tags list segmentation; the piece is a field review, not a new algorithm.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly neuroscience suddenly has both genetic remote controls and electron-microscope wiring diagrams. This review asks how to put those maps together—and how long a full adult-brain connectome will take if computers, not only people, do the tracing.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical neuropil has about one chemical synapse per cubic micrometre, so dense connectomes need to call millions to billions of synapses. Faster neurite reconstruction has made synapse annotation the new bottleneck.
ocar.challenge: Detection is easy in high-resolution FIB-SEM or extracellular-space-enhanced tissue, but large-scale mapping uses conventional en-bloc-stained, lower-resolution 3D EM in which most neurite contacts are non-synaptic.
ocar.action: Staffler, Berning, Boergens, Gour, van der Smagt and Helmstaedter, in eLife (2017), introduce SynEM: given a neurite segmentation, classify interfaces as synaptic or not, recovering location, size, partners, and direction without a user.
ocar.resolution: They report 97% precision and recall on binary cortical connectomes with no interaction, outperforming contemporaneous methods even on high-resolution anisotropic data. Inhibitory versus excitatory assignment can use the parent axon when many of its synapses are in the volume.
ocar.future_work: They argue the method scales to large cortical volumes and plausibly whole-brain datasets, removing manual synapse annotation as a bottleneck for dense mammalian connectomes.

summaries.beginner: A speck of cortex contains enormous numbers of synapses, too many to click by hand once the wires are traced. SynEM is a program that looks at each place two processes touch and decides whether it is a real synapse, without a person in the loop.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2017), Staffler, Berning, Boergens, Gour, van der Smagt and Helmstaedter present SynEM for automated synapse detection in conventionally stained 3D EM. Rather than searching voxels de novo, it classifies borders from an existing segmentation as synaptic or not, yielding location, size, neurites, and direction. They report 97% precision and recall on binary cortical connectomes without user interaction. The method is aimed at scalable, lower-resolution volumes, not only FIB-SEM. Axon-level aggregation can label inhibitory versus excitatory synapses when interneuron axons are contained in the block.
summaries.advanced: 97% is for the binary connectome after their operating point, not a claim of zero error on synapse size. Catalog abstract text says 98% and that 80–90% of synapses are excitatory; the published PDF abstract in this extract uses 97% and omits that excitatory fraction. Performance depends on segmentation quality. Extracellular-space protocols would make the task easier; SynEM is built for conventional fixation where touch is usually non-synaptic.

plain_language_summary: A speck of cortex contains enormous numbers of synapses, too many to click by hand once the wires are traced. SynEM is a program that looks at each place two processes touch and decides whether it is a real synapse, without a person in the loop.

ocar.opportunity: Parallel-fiber systems such as cerebellum and the insect mushroom body associate stimuli with reinforcement, but no complete synaptic wiring diagram of such a circuit had been available.
ocar.challenge: Whether Kenyon-cell input from projection neurons is purely random, how compartments implement learning, and how output neurons interact were open, and larva versus adult homology needed a full map.
ocar.action: Eichler, Li, Litwin-Kumar, Park, Andrade, Schneider-Mizell, Saumweber, Huser, Eschbach, Gerber, Fetter, Truman, Priebe, Abbott, Thum, Zlatic and Cardona reconstruct the complete first-instar Drosophila larval mushroom body at synaptic resolution from serial-section EM (bioRxiv 2017; catalogued as Nature).
ocar.resolution: Most Kenyon cells mix random projection-neuron inputs; a subset gets stereotyped single-PN input—an organization that maximizes a model output neuron’s stimulus discrimination. Each compartment has a canonical motif including reciprocal KC–modulatory synapses, modulatory→output synapses, and many recurrent KC–KC contacts. Stereotyped MBON–MBON connections could aid selection of learned behaviors. KC→modulatory synapse numbers are comparable to KC→MBON.
ocar.future_work: The map is offered to guide functional tests. Glutamatergic MBON–MBON links are hypothesized to be inhibitory by analogy to adult work but need physiological confirmation. Basic architecture is expected to generalize across larval/adult Drosophila and other insects even if individual neurons remodel at metamorphosis.

summaries.beginner: Young fruit-fly maggots already learn to like or avoid odors using a brain structure called the mushroom body. This paper traces every synapse in that structure and finds both random mixing of odor inputs and extra loops among the cells that teach and remember.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2017 reconstruction (bioRxiv; catalog venue Nature), Eichler, Li, Litwin-Kumar, Zlatic, Cardona and colleagues map the complete Drosophila first-instar mushroom body. Most Kenyon cells integrate random combinations of projection neurons, while a subset receives stereotyped single-PN input; that mix maximizes model discrimination. Beyond classic KC→MBON and modulatory→KC synapses they find reciprocal KC–modulatory contacts, modulatory→MBON synapses, abundant recurrent KC–KC connections, and a structured MBON–MBON network consistent with mutual inhibition between opposite learned valences. First-instar larvae already show associative learning.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal is Nature while the uuid is the bioRxiv preprint; content matches the published larval MB connectome. ‘Complete’ is for this L1 MB, not the whole larval CNS. Randomness of PN→KC wiring is constrained by the full bilateral map but remains a model of development. Signs of MBON transmitters (glutamate, GABA) used to infer inhibition need functional tests. Visual PN inputs are reported here as new for larva.

plain_language_summary: Young fruit-fly maggots already learn to like or avoid odors using a brain structure called the mushroom body. This paper traces every synapse in that structure and finds both random mixing of odor inputs and extra loops among the cells that teach and remember.

ocar.opportunity: Dense mammalian connectomes need much faster neurite reconstruction than earlier desktop tools allowed, including by trained annotator crowds working over the web.
ocar.challenge: Existing annotation software limited the volumes that could realistically be mapped.
ocar.action: Boergens, Berning, Bocklisch, Bräunlein, Drawitsch, Frohnhofen, Herold, Otto, Rzepka, Werkmeister, Werner, Wiese, Wissler and Helmstaedter, in Nature Methods, present webKnossos, an in-browser 3D EM annotation tool whose ‘flight mode’ is a single-view egocentric reconstruction method.
ocar.resolution: Trained crowds reconstruct at 1.5 ± 0.6 mm/h for axons and 2.1 ± 0.9 mm/h for dendrites in mammalian cortical 3D EM. That is a 4- to 13-fold acceleration versus then-current state-of-the-art tools.
ocar.future_work: The authors state that this speed extends the range of connectomes that can realistically be mapped.

summaries.beginner: Tracing nerve fibers in 3D microscope data is usually done with clunky desktop software. webKnossos lets people fly through the volume in a browser, and trained tracers move several times faster than with earlier tools.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods, Boergens, Berning, Helmstaedter and colleagues introduce webKnossos, an in-browser annotation tool for 3D electron microscopy. Flight mode is a single-view egocentric reconstruction style used by trained annotator crowds. They report 1.5 ± 0.6 mm per hour on axons and 2.1 ± 0.9 mm per hour on dendrites in mammalian cortex, a 4- to 13-fold speedup relative to contemporaneous tools. The aim is to enlarge the set of connectomes that can actually be finished.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF extract is not this article, so this card uses the catalog abstract. Speeds are means ± variation for trained annotators on cortical EM, not a guarantee for novices or other tissues. The comparison baseline is not named in the abstract. Catalog year is 2017.

plain_language_summary: Tracing nerve fibers in 3D microscope data is usually done with clunky desktop software. webKnossos lets people fly through the volume in a browser, and trained tracers move several times faster than with earlier tools.

ocar.opportunity: Dense reconstructions of neuronal populations enable cell-type, projection, and circuit analyses. Serial block-face EM can deliver ultrastructural resolution through large volumes if charging is controlled.
ocar.challenge: Sample charging degrades SBEM signal. Tracing thousands of olfactory-bulb neurons by hand still requires efficient software and error correction.
ocar.action: Wanner, Genoud and Friedrich, in Scientific Data (2016), acquire an SBEM stack of a zebrafish larva olfactory bulb at 9.25 × 9.25 × 25 nm³ using conductive silver particles in the surrounding resin, then manually skeletonize neurons in a new Python tool, PyKNOSSOS.
ocar.resolution: Skeletons of 1,022 neurons—98% of olfactory-bulb neurons—were reconstructed. The density supports geometrical and topological circuit analyses; data are served via neurodata.io and viewable in PyKNOSSOS. Conductive embedding allowed high-vacuum imaging and improved signal-to-noise.
ocar.future_work: They propose merging these skeletons with automated supervoxels for volumetric reconstructions, building an integrated molecular–anatomical–functional atlas, comparing glomerular classes (including pheromonal glomeruli), and mapping organelles and synapses onto identified cells.

summaries.beginner: The nose-brain of a baby zebrafish is small enough that almost every neuron can be traced in an electron-microscope stack. This data paper releases those pictures and 1,022 cell skeletons, plus software to browse them.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Data (2016), Wanner, Genoud and Friedrich report SBEM of a larval zebrafish olfactory bulb at 9.25 × 9.25 × 25 nm³ voxels, using silver particles in the resin to cut charging and allow high-vacuum imaging. Manual tracing with efficient error correction produced skeletons of 1,022 neurons, 98% of neurons in the bulb. PyKNOSSOS supports browsing, tracing, synapse annotation, and visualization. Image data are available through neurodata.io. The density of reconstructions is intended for morphology, projection, and circuit topology studies.
summaries.advanced: These are skeletons, not a full volumetric segmentation or a complete synapse list; the authors explicitly leave dense volumes to a later supervoxel-plus-skeleton merge. ‘98% of all neurons in the OB’ is their census of this larval bulb. Subglomerular innervation by mitral cells is a preliminary observation. Catalog method is SBF-SEM, matching SBEM.

plain_language_summary: The nose-brain of a baby zebrafish is small enough that almost every neuron can be traced in an electron-microscope stack. This data paper releases those pictures and 1,022 cell skeletons, plus software to browse them.
